title: Nobody Here Is Wrong
logline: A coastal peat marsh with no landmark higher than a reed, crossed every day by three completely different ideas of how to get through it: a two-hundred-year-old cargo canal ruled dead straight, a fan of fishermen's channels that branch and close and open again, and an expressway that stands on piers where there is open water and, over the peat itself, on ground that had to be drained and piled before it would carry anything at all.
human_question: When several people point different ways and every one of them is right, what exactly is it that you do not know?

place.what_kind_of_place: A large coastal peat marsh and lagoon system on a flat stretch of coast, wedged between a lagoon mouth at one end and a river at the other. It is a working place rather than an empty one: people fish it, set traps in it and move through it daily by small boat. Three routes cross it and none of them can see the others properly. The oldest is a colonial cargo canal cut straight through the peat two centuries ago and still holding its line. The commonest are the fishermen's channels, which are not engineered at all, which branch endlessly, and which silt up, grow over and reopen with the water level and the season. The newest is an expressway, which crosses the open water on piers and, over the peat itself, runs on an embankment that had to be pre-loaded, drained and stone-piled before the ground would hold it — at a height and a speed from which the marsh is scenery.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: It is the rare landscape that denies the camera the one thing a camera usually gives you for free, which is orientation. At boat height inside the reed channels there is no horizon, no landmark and nothing above head height: every frame looks like every other frame, and the only way to know you have turned is that the light has moved. Then the drone climbs forty metres and the same place becomes one of the most beautiful patterns in the country: a green labyrinth of water branching and rebranching with no centre and no edge, and cut across it, absolutely straight, a line of water somebody ruled with an instrument, and above that a grey concrete line on legs with traffic on it. Three answers to one question, in one frame, at three heights.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The water, the reeds and the traffic, on three completely different clocks. The channels change with the tide twice a day and with the rains across a season: a route that worked last month is a wall of reed this month, and a wall of reed last year is a route now. The canal changes on the scale of decades and mostly by silting. The expressway does not change at all, and its traffic never stops. Birds lift off the marsh in numbers at dawn and again at dusk. Nothing here can be scheduled except the tide and the light.
place.when_it_looks_best: The first hour after sunrise, when mist is still sitting on the channels and the water takes the sky, and the last hour before dark, when the straight canal goes silver and the expressway lights come on above a marsh that has gone black. A falling tide opens more channel and exposes more bank; the two monsoon shoulders give the most dramatic differences between one month's route and the next.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A wetland film built on a single visual joke that the landscape makes by itself: an enormous green maze with two straight lines drawn through it. It resolves without any commentary at all, from mist at dawn through a working day on the water to the expressway lights coming on over a black marsh. There is bird noise, boat noise, reed noise and traffic noise, and there are aerials that people will watch twice. Anyone who has no interest whatsoever in philosophy gets a complete piece.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same marsh becomes a careful piece of argument that never accuses anyone. The sources describe a mind that cannot come to a decision about the thing in front of it, and they are unusually careful to separate that from the ordinary state of not knowing something you have no way of finding out yet, which one of them says may not be a fault at all. This place lets a film hold that distinction open rather than settle it, because here the not-knowing is genuinely in the ground: the marsh withholds direction from everybody equally, three different answers are all in daily use, and not one of them is a mistake. The voice reads the water and the reeds, and says plainly that it cannot see inside anybody.

sequence.on_screen: Dawn, drone at boat height, moving slowly up a reed channel. Walls of reed on both sides, mist on the water, no horizon, nothing above head height. The shot runs long enough to become uncomfortable.
sequence.voice: There is no landmark in here. Not a low one, not a distant one, none. The reeds are taller than a standing person and they are the same on all sides. You can be a hundred metres from a main channel or a kilometre, and the view is identical.

sequence.on_screen: The drone climbs hard out of the channel. The maze opens out: hundreds of branching waterways in green peat, no centre, no edge, going to the horizon.
sequence.voice: From up here it is obvious that there is no single way through, because there are thousands. People who work this marsh every day will give you different routes, and the reason they differ is not that some of them are wrong. It is that each one learned the water at a different level, in a different month.

sequence.on_screen: The old canal, from directly above: a perfectly straight line of water running through the maze from edge of frame to edge of frame, ignoring every bend in the peat.
sequence.voice: Two hundred years ago somebody decided the marsh should have an answer, and cut one. Straight, surveyed, for cargo. It is still here and it still works, and it still has nothing to say about any of the water on either side of it.

sequence.on_screen: The expressway: concrete piers standing in marsh water, the deck above, traffic crossing at speed. Then the reverse angle from the water, looking up at the underside as a boat passes beneath.
sequence.voice: And then the third answer, which solved the problem by refusing it. Nobody up there is navigating this marsh. They are going over it at a hundred kilometres an hour, and from that height the question does not exist.

sequence.on_screen: One high wide frame that holds all three at once: maze, ruled canal, elevated road, with a small boat working somewhere in the middle of it.
sequence.voice: Three ways across one piece of ground, in use on the same morning, none of them a mistake. The texts have a careful line about this. The doubt they warn about is a specific thing, a stalling about eight matters of religion, and they say straight out that the ordinary state of not knowing something you cannot yet look into is not that, and may not be a fault at all [C008-P:L36; C074-P:L404]. They do not say how the two are related. Neither does this film, and neither does this marsh.

sequence.on_screen: A channel that simply ends: reed grown right across it, water going nowhere, a boat turning in its own length. Then a different channel, open this month, that was closed last year.
sequence.voice: What the texts do describe is the shape of a mind that cannot land on its object [C008-P:L34], and they add something easy to miss about how it feels. It feels like nothing. Not bad, not good, flat, because you cannot like or dislike what you have not got hold of [C008-P:L30]. That is worth saying carefully. A flat feeling is not a peaceful one, and the sources are explicit that this greyness is not the calm of wisdom.

sequence.on_screen: Working the marsh in ordinary daylight: traps lifted, a channel poled through, two boats meeting and passing, one crew calling something across to another.
sequence.voice: The remedies the compendium lists against the states that cover the mind are not heroic. Be widely learned. Ask a great many questions. Keep the company of people who know more and talk with them at the right time [C074-P:L366–L380]. Asking the way is not the failure. In a place with no landmarks, asking the way is the whole method.

sequence.on_screen: Dusk. The marsh goes black, the straight canal holds the last silver light, the expressway lamps come on in a line above it. Birds going down into the reeds.
sequence.voice: The marsh will not tell anyone which way to go. It has never told anyone. That is not a defect in the people crossing it, and this film makes no claim at all about what is in anyone's mind, because a camera cannot see that. It can only show a place that withholds, and three honest answers to it.

concept_merge.why_together: C008 supplies the state and, just as importantly, the limit on it. Its general description of doubt is a mind that cannot reach a decision about its object, which counts as a hindrance because it obstructs doing good [C008-P:L34]; it explains why such a mind always carries a flat, neutral feeling, since what has not been grasped can be neither enjoyed nor disliked [C008-P:L30]; and it then draws a hard line, saying the doubt it condemns is uncertainty about eight specific religious matters and that ordinary not-knowing about something one cannot yet investigate is not that doubt at all [C008-P:L36]. C074 confirms the line independently, naming the ordinary kind look-alike doubt and saying it may well not be unwholesome [C074-P:L404], and then supplies the remedies, which are flatly practical: be widely learned, ask many questions, keep the company of elders and talk about suitable things at the right time [C074-P:L366–L380]. Put on a marsh where direction is genuinely unavailable, the state and its remedy stop being a diagnosis and a technique and become the ordinary daily conduct of everyone working the water.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That not knowing the way and asking the way are the same activity, and that a film can show the first without accusing anybody of the second. C008 on its own would make the not-knowing look like a fault the camera has caught. C074 on its own would make the asking look like a self-improvement tip. Together, and on this ground, they produce the group's most precise statement: the information is missing from the landscape, not from the people. And the place makes it visible at three scales at once, a maze that gives no direction, a ruled line that imposes one, and a road that declines the question, all inside a single frame.

concept_links.why: The general description in the sources is a mind that, under a darkening that prevents knowing a matter as it is [C008-M:L3], cannot come to a decision about its object, and which counts as a hindrance because it blocks wholesome action [C008-P:L34]. The film shows the everyday shape of that, and nothing else: it shows a place that withholds direction. Two guards from the digest are load-bearing and are carried on screen rather than only in the notes. First, the harmful doubt the sources mean is restricted to eight named religious matters and is separated explicitly from the honest not-knowing of something one has no way to investigate [C008-P:L36]; the digest also records as unresolved how the general and the restricted definitions relate, so beat 5 states the restriction, states that the sources do not join the two, and asserts nothing about which kind anything on screen might be. Second, the neutral feeling these states carry is a dull greyness from failing to grasp the object and is not equanimity [C008-P:L30], which beat 6 says outright so that the film's own low, drifting tone cannot be mistaken for calm. The film also never presents anyone in frame as an instance of a state, because a camera cannot see which factor is present.

The compendium independently makes the same distinction, calling ordinary uncertainty about an unknown matter look-alike doubt and saying it may not be unwholesome at all, as against the hindrance-doubt about the eight matters [C074-P:L404], which is why this link is what lets the film be generous rather than diagnostic. It then supplies the helps listed against these covering states, which are entirely ordinary: wide learning, asking many questions, and keeping the company of elders and suitable conversation [C074-P:L366–L380]. This link is therefore to the remedy, not to the defilement. The digest's own limits are honoured: abandonment in these sources is staged and technical rather than a decision, so the film promises nobody a way out of the marsh; the stakes in the source are not stress or productivity, so no wellbeing language is used; and the corrected citation matters, since the earlier draft attached the remedies to the line that actually carries the look-alike-doubt distinction.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That not knowing which way to go is not in itself the thing the old texts warn about. They restrict that to a short list of religious questions and say in as many words that honest not-knowing about something you cannot yet find out is a different matter. What they do describe is the shape of a mind that cannot land on anything, and the odd fact that it feels like nothing at all, which is not the same as feeling calm. And the answer they give is not resolve or effort. It is ask, and keep company with people who know.
what_must_be_real: The marsh, the channels, the canal and the road, and the work that goes on in the water. Nothing is arranged: no route is cleared, no channel is cut or blocked, no boat is asked to go somewhere it was not going, no one is asked to point or to give directions for the camera, and no one's day is lengthened by the filming. Nobody in frame is presented as lost, mistaken or confused, and no answer anyone gives is set against anyone else's to make one of them look foolish. The differences between routes are shown as facts about water levels and seasons, which is what they are. Birds and nesting are not disturbed for a shot.
position_hint: opening candidate for the group: it is the plainest possible first step, a place that genuinely withholds direction, and it sets the low, drifting tone while establishing at the outset that the film is describing ground rather than judging people. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Making helpful, skilled people look foolish or lost, when the missing information is in the landscape and not in them.

Narrating the three routes as a progress story, primitive to modern, with the fishermen's channels as the old way that the canal and the expressway improved on. The film's whole argument is that the three are contemporaries and none is behind: the channels are in daily use, they are the only one of the three still being revised, and the survey that recorded them calls their methods sustainable. Any beat that orders the routes in time as though that ordered them in merit destroys the film.

Enjoying the colonial engineering failure. The record is that a cut was made to improve this ground and let the sea into it; that is stated as what happened. No colonial power is named as the culprit beyond what the source being followed names, the local nickname for the canal is reported as a nickname rather than endorsed, and nobody is called a fool.

Overstating the expressway. Much of its crossing is embankment on treated peat, not deck on legs; the named viaducts are short and at the ends. 'A road that goes over the whole thing without touching it' is the film's shorthand and it exceeds the record, so the shots have to earn it or the shorthand has to go.

Claiming the sources' harmful doubt for what is on screen. It is restricted to eight religious matters, the digest records the relation between the general and restricted definitions as unresolved, and the film must assert nothing about which kind of not-knowing it is showing.
Reading the flat, drifting mood as calm; the digest is explicit that the neutral feeling in these states is not equanimity, and this group's tone makes that an easy mistake.
Sliding into a staged metaphor, a travel piece or a boat tour, or letting a hired guide become a narrator in all but name.
Treating the expressway, the canal or the local channels as the right answer and the other two as errors; the whole film depends on all three being honest.
Consent from people working on the water who appear briefly and in passing, and the possibility that a crew's presence alters whether anyone offers help.
Disturbing birds or nesting in a protected wetland for an aerial shot, and drone restrictions near an expressway and an airport approach.

Aestheticising a wetland that is under real pressure from filling and encroachment without acknowledging it, and equally, campaigning. The filling, the dumping, the power-project land and the boundary litigation are recorded as dated disputes with no villain.
drop_if: The channels turn out to be signed, mapped or otherwise easy to read, so the place no longer withholds anything.
The three routes cannot be held in one frame, which is the film's single strongest image.

There is no reachable stretch where the expressway is genuinely a deck over water with a boat able to pass beneath it, so the third route can only be filmed as an embankment and the film loses its contrast between crossing and going over.
Filming can only happen as a chartered tour with a guide performing the marsh for the camera.
Aerial permission over the wetland or near the expressway is refused.

connections.note: Takes in the costly-decision strand and the guard that separates honest not-knowing from the doubt the sources warn about, now carried by the place rather than by a person.
Two surfaces that withhold: one hides what is under it, the other hides which way to go.
A route that will not resolve, and a circle that cannot be left.

selection.reason: Carries the group's opening by putting the not-knowing in the ground rather than in a person, and holds three honest answers to one question in a single frame. Legacy merge recommendations (IDEA-0056) were cleared on 2026-09-25: they came from the retired pre-rewrite review reports, which argued merges while ideas competed for episode slots. Those reports are retired, every idea is now 'keep', and selection happens through Chathura's verdict against a per-group quota. The named ideas still exist as separate candidates with their own locations, so the merge was never executed. This field now records executed merges only.

review.note: Rewritten 2026-09-22 into the footage-led shape and rebuilt from the ground up. The old version followed a lost traveller asking strangers, which the no-protagonist rule forbids; the film now has no traveller at all and is set in a marsh that genuinely withholds direction, with three routes across it whose disagreement is a fact about water levels and seasons. Both digests re-read fresh: C074's remedies were re-cited from L366-L380, since the earlier draft had attached them to L404, which actually carries the look-alike-doubt distinction, and that distinction is now on screen in beat 5. The guard that this flat feeling is not equanimity is stated in the narration rather than only listed as a risk. A proposed location was added. Research added to suggested_location 2026-09-25 with no change to the logline, two_layers, sequence, concept_merge or concept_links, and no new citations. A historical_thread was written giving all three routes and the marsh a dated record: the paddy land and the cut that admitted the sea, the pre-Dutch, Dutch and British canals with Gavin Hamilton's career and death, the 2013 expressway and how its crossing of the peat was actually engineered, and the wetland's present status from the 1989 development freeze through the 1991 master plan and the 1996 sanctuary to the 2021 gazette and the Court of Appeal's boundary direction. The drainage-and-salinisation account is established in substance and contested in attribution, and what_is_disputed sets out all four attributions rather than choosing one. Three earlier assertions were corrected: the marsh is 3,068 ha and not about 6,000; the British canal is a second parallel cut and not a widening of the Dutch line; and the expressway crosses much of the marsh on treated embankment rather than on piers, which makes the film's 'road on legs over the whole thing' shorthand an overstatement — recorded as a risk, a drop_if and an unknown rather than silently rewritten into the logline, because that is Chathura's call. Two images added and all six confirmed. Verdict unchanged and still pending: the film and its place are the same. Corrected on 2026-09-25 after the research pass: the logline and place block had the expressway crossing the marsh on piers 'without touching it', which the construction record does not support — the viaducts are at the two ends and most of the length sits on treated peat. Both were rewritten to the record. The film is not weakened by it and is arguably sharper: the third answer did not go over this ground, it went into it and had to re-engineer it before it would bear weight, which makes the three routes cut through, thread through, and stand on, rather than two on the ground and one above it.

suggested_location.name: Muthurajawela marsh, the Hamilton Canal and the elevated crossing of the Colombo-Katunayake Expressway

also_known_as.name: Muthurajawela
also_known_as.meaning: glossed in popular usage as 'supreme field of pearls' or 'swamp of royal treasure'; R. L. Brohier instead derives it from the mutu-samba or 'pearl rice' the fields here once produced
also_known_as.used_by: Sinhala usage; the Brohier derivation is the only one carrying a source

also_known_as.name: the Dutch Canal, Paru Ela
also_known_as.meaning: the older canal line east of the British one, begun before the Dutch and extended by them; Paru Ela is the barge canal
also_known_as.used_by: local and tourist usage; both names are also applied loosely to the British canal

also_known_as.name: Moda Ela, Hamilton's Folly
also_known_as.meaning: the fool's canal: a nickname reported for the British canal on the ground that it increased the salt it was cut to remove
also_known_as.used_by: widely repeated in travel and blog sources; not found in the Brohier-based accounts

suggested_location.region: The coastal strip of Gampaha district, Western Province, between the Negombo lagoon mouth and the Kelani river, just inland of the airport road
suggested_location.why_here: It is the only candidate found that supplies the concept, the spectacle and a datable history in the same frame. The marsh itself runs to 3,068 hectares and is the largest saline coastal peat bog in the country; with the lagoon at its northern end (3,164 ha) it forms one wetland system of 6,232 ha, and the whole of it is a genuine labyrinth with no landmark above reed height, worked daily by fishing families who each know it by a different set of channels. Onto that exact piece of ground three incompatible ideas of a route have been laid, each one datable. A colonial cargo canal, 14.5 km cut dead straight in 1802-04 and still navigated, which was built to take salt water out of the marsh and is widely said to have let more in. A fan of fishermen's channels that are not engineered at all and that close and open with the water level. And an expressway opened in 2013 which crosses the marsh partly on treated fill and partly on decks carried over water, and whose drivers are not navigating anything. Three answers, one place, all in use on the same morning, and they can be held in one aerial frame. Behind all three sits the oldest answer of all: the record that this ground was paddy land, that somebody cut a channel to protect it, and that the channel let the sea in and ended the cultivation. That is both the best shot the location produces and the clearest statement the group's concepts have anywhere.

historical_thread.story:
The place is a coastal peat basin lying between the Negombo lagoon and the Kelani river and reaching inland as far as Ragama and Peliyagoda, in Gampaha District. IUCN's biodiversity survey fixes it at 7°03'N, 79°55'E and calls it the largest saline coastal peat bog in Sri Lanka. The marsh covers 3,068 ha; with the Negombo lagoon (3,164 ha) it makes a single coastal wetland system of 6,232 ha, estimated to have formed about 5000 BC. Its main freshwater source is the Dandugam Oya, which drains a catchment of 727 km², and it takes 2,000-2,500 mm of rain a year.

The name. R. L. Brohier derives Muthurajawela from the mutu-samba, the pearly white 'pearl rice' that these fields were said to produce in abundance every year. The glosses in general circulation — 'supreme field of pearls', 'swamp of royal treasure' — are repeated everywhere and attached to no source; Brohier's is the only derivation found with a book behind it.

The paddy, and the cut that ended it. 'According to historical evidence, Muthurajawela was subjected to extensive cultivation of paddy, more than 500 years ago' — the Greater Colombo Economic Commission and Euroconsult master plan of 1991, quoted by IUCN. Brohier describes the ground: paddy running for kilometres along a line of sand dunes that separated the fields from the sea on one side, with higher ground on the other, the higher ground the Colombo-Negombo road now runs on. On his account the first canal here was begun by the Portuguese, some time in their period of 1505-1656, excavating from the Kelani Ganga in order to divert the river's floodwater away from the paddy. It did not work, and it did not merely fail: the cut 'unintentionally created a passage through which saline seawater entered the agricultural lands, leading to the destruction of the paddy fields'. The fields were abandoned. The standard account adds that the Dutch later tried paddy in the marsh themselves and found, as Sinhalese kings had before them, that the coastal tides inundated the fields with sea water.

The first route: the canal. The Dutch, between 1658 and 1795, took the abandoned Portuguese cut and made it do something it could do — carry goods. Records of 1706 have the canal already reaching the Maha Oya; within that decade further cuts joined rivers, lagoons and backwaters into a continuous water route from Colombo to Puttalam of about 193 km, with 24 km more across the Puttalam lagoon to Kalpitiya, and they brought in the flat-bottomed padda boat. The system, at its maximum, is also given as 172 km. Cinnamon went down it in barges to the port at Negombo. After the British took the coast in 1796 a second canal was cut, parallel to the Dutch line and nearer the sea: begun in 1802, finished in 1804, 14.5 km from the mouth of the Kelani Ganga at Hekitta to the southern edge of the Negombo lagoon at Pamunugama, wide enough for two-way traffic. Its stated purpose was to drain salt water out of the marsh. It is named after Gavin Hamilton, Agent of Revenue and Commerce for the District of Colombo, who had come out with Frederick North, the first British governor, in 1798, was private secretary first to the Colonial Secretary Hugh Cleghorn and then to North, was made Acting Civil Paymaster in April 1799 and Deputy Paymaster General in 1802, and succeeded Joseph Greenhill as Agent of Revenue and Commerce. He died in February 1803, a year before the canal was finished, and after his death was found to have embezzled £19,675. Plans to extend the works and reclaim further land were dropped because of the war with the Kandyan kingdom. The widely repeated verdict on the canal is that it produced the reverse of its purpose — that it 'created the opposite effect, as the coastal tides brought increasing salinity not only from Negombo Lagoon but also the Kelani Ganga' — and that it is known locally as Moda Ela, the fool's canal, and as Hamilton's Folly. When the Puttalam-Colombo railway opened in 1926 the water route was abandoned. The Sri Lanka Land Reclamation and Development Corporation began rehabilitating the canal in 2012, completing a 2.5 km section between Hekiththa junction and Pinwatta on 2 August 2013 at a cost of Rs 400 million.

Whoever is responsible, the ground never came back, and the process is not finished. IUCN's economic assessment records that 'due to the salinity, acidity and low natural fertility of its predominantly peat soils, the marsh area is unsuitable for cultivating all but a very few crops' — roughly 60 ha under coconut, 20 ha under bananas and 14 ha under vegetables in a marsh of 3,068 ha. And IUCN's water-quality survey found the intrusion still running: when flow in the Dandugam Oya, the Ja-Ela canal and the Hamilton canal falls in the low-rain period, saline water penetrates into the marsh and both salinity and pH rise.

The second route: the channels. IUCN recorded a small number of traditional fishing families working the canals, the Dandugam Oya and the marsh-lagoon transition zone with hook and rod, drift nets, cast nets and brush piles, mainly for cichlids — tilapia, orange chromide and pearl spot — and described those methods in terms as 'sustainable practices'. Reeds and sedges cut in the marsh are used for fish traps, mats and handicrafts. Fisheries account for 36% of the wetland's resource-use value and agriculture for 41%. Almost 300,000 people live in the wider marsh-and-lagoon area; just under 5,000 live in or immediately beside the marsh, and the households inside the conservation zone rose from 52 in 1952 to about 700 by 2002.

The third route: the expressway. 25.8 km from Colombo to the airport at Katunayake. An earlier contract awarded to a Korean consortium in 1999 was terminated in January 2003; the agreement with China Metallurgical Group Corporation was signed on 17 August 2008, loan agreements on 6 August 2009, and construction ran from 2009 to the opening on 27 October 2013 by President Mahinda Rajapaksa. The total cost was US$292 million, of which US$248.2 million came from the Exim Bank of China. The speed limit is 80 km/h for the first eight kilometres and 100 km/h after that. Its line runs from the marshes at Peliyagoda over paddy and marsh to the eastern edge of the Muthurajawela marsh, then north 'generally parallel and sometimes over the Old Dutch Canal', over the eastern edge of the Negombo lagoon — 1.4 km of it through the lagoon itself — with bridges over the Dandugam Oya and Ja-Ela. A major part of the route crosses flood plain and marsh of soft peat, organic soil and clay up to fifty feet thick, and peat, being spongy, can collapse when loaded. The crossing was therefore not simply banked up: the project used pre-loading and surcharging, prefabricated vertical drains, sand compaction piles and stone columns, and carries 42 bridges and between 88 and 102 culverts built mostly over the marshes, with a 480 m viaduct at Hunupitiya and an 800 m viaduct at Katunayake. The newest answer is therefore part road on treated peat and part deck on legs, and where it stands on legs it stands on legs because the ground will not hold a road.

The present status. Scott and Poole listed the wetland in 1989 as one of Sri Lanka's twelve priority wetlands. In 1989 the government froze public and private development in the marsh pending a master plan; the Greater Colombo Economic Commission and Euroconsult produced it in 1991, zoning 160 ha (2.5%) as mixed urban, 400 ha as a recreational buffer, the fringes for settlement, and about 85% as conservation area, and the government accepted it in 1992. In July 1996, 1,777 ha of the northern section was declared a sanctuary under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance, by Gazette 947/13, administered by the Department of Wildlife Conservation. IUCN's survey of November 1999 to April 2000 recorded 192 species of flora in seven vegetation communities — marsh, lentic flora, reed swamp, short grassland, shrubland, stream-bank flora and mangrove swamp — and 209 vertebrates: 40 fish, 14 amphibians, 31 reptiles, 102 birds and 22 mammals, of which 17 are endemic and 26 nationally threatened, with 36 new records; also 48 butterflies and 22 dragonflies. Up to 75 ha of the northern marsh is mangrove. The same survey recorded the threats: illegal filling and reclamation, clearing of vegetation, deliberate burning of scrub, large-scale garbage dumping, agro-chemicals from leaf-vegetable plots, sewage and pig and poultry farm waste, oil in the transition zone, poaching, harvesting of small fish for the aquarium trade, tree-cutting for illicit distilling, and eleven dominant invasive plants; and it found migrant bird numbers considerably down over ten years. The wetland's direct and indirect economic value was put at Rs 726.5 million a year, 90% of it ecosystem services, chiefly flood attenuation and waste-water treatment — the marsh holds up to 11 million cubic metres and discharges to the lagoon and the sea by way of the Hamilton Canal.

The disputes are documented and current. Gazette 1466/26 of 13 October 2006 declared 206.678 ha an Environmental Protection Area; a later gazette, 2090/11, declared 162.10 ha while removing 44.578 ha, about 110 acres, for a liquefied-natural-gas power project. On 7 October 2021 a gazette placed roughly 1,447 ha under the Urban Development Authority, presented as a step towards declaring a protected Ramsar wetland; it drew protests across the Western Province, a Supreme Court petition from the Archbishop of Colombo, Cardinal Malcolm Ranjith, and objections from ministers and members of parliament, and the government appointed a review committee to revisit the boundaries. Writ petitions by Cardinal Ranjith and by the Centre for Environmental Justice, filed in January 2021, led a two-judge Court of Appeal bench to direct the Surveyor General to expedite the demarcation of the sanctuary's physical boundaries, with undertakings from the Director-General of Wildlife to demarcate Blocks 1 and 2 and from the Central Environmental Authority to mark the southern and western environmental-protection boundaries, both within six months. The sanctuary had been gazetted in 1996 and its boundaries had never been marked on the ground; in the meantime a private company had marked parts of the wetland as its own property.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
The concepts here are a state and its remedy, and the history on this ground supplies both without the film having to look inside anybody.

Start with what C008's Pradeepika actually says. Delusion is a darkening that prevents knowing a matter as it is; doubt is a mind that cannot reach a decision about its object, and it counts as a hindrance because it obstructs wholesome action. But the same text restricts the doubt it condemns to eight religious matters and says plainly that the ordinary not-knowing of something one has no way to investigate is not that doubt; C074 says the same independently, calling the ordinary kind look-alike doubt and allowing that it may not be unwholesome. The digest records that the sources never explain how the general definition and the restricted one are related. So the film's job is to hold a distinction open, not to diagnose anything — and this ground holds it open by itself, because here the missing information is demonstrably in the landscape. The peat is flat, the reed is the tallest thing in it, the channels change with the tide twice a day and with the rains across a season, and the ground's own salinity moves with the flow in the canals. Nobody on the water is failing to know something knowable. They are reading a place that withholds.

Then the history does the thing no analogy could. Three routes cross this marsh, each of them a confident answer to the same question, each contradicting the others, and all three still in use on the same morning. The canal answers by ruling a line and ignoring the water on both sides of it. The channels answer by having no line at all and being relearned every season. The expressway answers by declining the question at eighty metres a second. The record does not rank them, and neither can the film: the twenty-five-kilometre road was laid, for part of its length, along and sometimes over the line of the oldest cut on the ground, so even the newest answer follows the oldest one; and where the newest answer stands on legs it stands on legs because the peat will not carry it, which is the marsh setting the terms, not the road.

And then the oldest answer of all, which is the spine. This was paddy. Somebody cut a channel to protect it, and the channel admitted the sea, and the cultivation ended, and four hundred years later the soil is still too saline and too acid to grow much of anything. That is not a film's metaphor; it is what the IUCN assessment says about the present-day ground. Then a second canal was cut, two hundred years ago, whose written purpose was to take the salt back out, and the most repeated verdict on it is that it brought more in. The confident answer made the ground worse; the tentative ones did not. C074 is the concept that lets the film say this without becoming an accusation. Its whole method is to name the same handful of states again under different images — something that ferments and leaks, a flood, a yoke, a knot, a grip, a lid over the mind — and then to list what helps, and what helps is ordinary to the point of anticlimax: be widely learned, ask a great many questions, keep the company of people who know more, talk about suitable things at the right time. Three routes across one marsh is what asking a great many questions looks like when it is done by generations instead of by a person. The fishermen's channels are asking. The canal is an answer that stopped asking. In a place with no landmark, asking the way is not the failure; it is the method, and it is the only one of the three that has been revised.

The limits are firm and they are the reason this binds rather than preaches. The colonial history is recorded, not adjudicated: what is said is that a cut was made and the sea came in, not that anyone was a fool, and the local nickname is reported as a nickname rather than endorsed. The three routes are not a sequence from primitive to modern, and the people who work the channels are not the old way — they are the ones whose answer is still being corrected, which by the compendium's own list of helps is the better position to be in, and IUCN's own description of their methods is 'sustainable practices'. The present-day disputes over filling, dumping and boundaries are recorded as disputes with dates and gazette numbers, and no side is narrated as right. And the film asserts nothing about anybody's mind, because C008's own digest says a camera cannot see which factor is present, and because the neutral feeling these states carry is a dull greyness from not grasping the object rather than any kind of calm — which is why the film's low tone has to be named as such rather than left to look like peace.
historical_thread.what_is_certain: That the marsh covers 3,068 ha, is the largest saline coastal peat bog in Sri Lanka, lies between the Negombo lagoon and the Kelani river in Gampaha District, and with the lagoon (3,164 ha) forms one wetland system of 6,232 ha; that its main freshwater source is the Dandugam Oya with a catchment of 727 km²; that annual rainfall is 2,000-2,500 mm. That it was paddy land, and that cultivation was abandoned because of salt-water intrusion — this is stated in the 1991 GCEC/Euroconsult master plan, quoted by IUCN, and is not in dispute in any source consulted. That the ground is still unfit for it: IUCN records that the predominantly peat soils are too saline, acid and infertile to grow all but a very few crops, with about 60 ha of coconut, 20 ha of bananas and 14 ha of vegetables in the whole marsh. That the intrusion is a live process, IUCN's water-quality survey finding saline water penetrating the marsh when flow in the Dandugam Oya, the Ja-Ela canal and the Hamilton canal falls in the low-rain period. That a canal system was built here across the whole colonial period for drainage and for cargo: a pre-Dutch cut from the Kelani Ganga, Dutch works between 1658 and 1795 that carried cinnamon in padda boats and reached the Maha Oya by 1706, and a British canal begun in 1802 and completed in 1804, 14.5 km long, running parallel to and west of the Dutch line from the mouth of the Kelani Ganga to the southern edge of the Negombo lagoon. That it is named after Gavin Hamilton, Agent of Revenue and Commerce for the District of Colombo, who came to Ceylon with Governor Frederick North in 1798, was private secretary to Hugh Cleghorn and then to North, became Acting Civil Paymaster in April 1799 and Deputy Paymaster General in 1802, died in February 1803 before the canal was finished, and was afterwards found to have embezzled £19,675. That the canal's stated purpose was to drain salt water out of the marsh. That the water route was abandoned after the Puttalam-Colombo railway opened in 1926, and that rehabilitation by the Sri Lanka Land Reclamation and Development Corporation began in 2012. That the expressway is 25.8 km long, was built by China Metallurgical Group Corporation under an agreement of 17 August 2008, cost US$292 million with US$248.2 million from the Exim Bank of China, and was opened on 27 October 2013 by President Mahinda Rajapaksa; that its speed limit is 80 km/h for eight kilometres and 100 km/h thereafter; that it runs over the eastern edge of the marsh, generally parallel to and sometimes over the old Dutch canal, and 1.4 km through the lagoon; that a major part of its length crosses soft peat, organic soil and clay up to fifty feet thick; that the ground was treated with pre-loading and surcharging, prefabricated vertical drains, sand compaction piles and stone columns; and that it carries 42 bridges, a 480 m viaduct at Hunupitiya and an 800 m viaduct at Katunayake. That development in the marsh was frozen in 1989, that a master plan was produced in 1991 by the Greater Colombo Economic Commission with Euroconsult and accepted in 1992, zoning about 85% as conservation area, and that in July 1996 1,777 ha of the northern section was declared a sanctuary under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance by Gazette 947/13. That IUCN's 1999-2000 survey recorded 192 flora across seven vegetation communities and 209 vertebrates (40 fish, 14 amphibians, 31 reptiles, 102 birds, 22 mammals), 17 endemic and 26 nationally threatened, plus 48 butterflies and 22 dragonflies. That the threats it recorded were filling and reclamation, clearing, burning, garbage dumping, agro-chemicals, sewage and farm waste, poaching, the aquarium-fish trade and invasive plants, and that migrant bird numbers had fallen. That the wetland's assessed economic value was Rs 726.5 million a year, 90% of it ecosystem services. That a few traditional fishing families work the canals, the Dandugam Oya and the transition zone with hook and rod, drift nets, cast nets and brush piles, mainly for tilapia, orange chromide and pearl spot, and that IUCN describes these as sustainable practices. That just under 5,000 people live in or beside the marsh out of almost 300,000 in the wider area. That the boundaries of the 1996 sanctuary were not demarcated on the ground, and that on writ petitions filed in January 2021 by Cardinal Malcolm Ranjith and the Centre for Environmental Justice the Court of Appeal directed the Surveyor General to expedite demarcation, with six-month undertakings from the Department of Wildlife Conservation and the Central Environmental Authority. That a gazette of 7 October 2021 placed part of the wetland under the Urban Development Authority, that it was protested and that a review committee was appointed.
historical_thread.what_is_disputed:
The name's meaning. Three glosses circulate: 'supreme field of pearls', 'swamp of royal treasure', and Brohier's derivation from mutu-samba, the pearly white 'pearl rice' the fields produced. Only the third carries a citation; the first two are repeated across travel writing and reference pages with no source attached, and a version invoking a legend of royalty and plundered riches appears with no source at all. The film should refer to the word by description and not settle the meaning.

Who cut the channel that let the sea in, and when. This is the single most contested point and it is the film's spine, so it is worth stating precisely. The account is established in substance — the fields were paddy, a cut admitted salt water, the cultivation ended — and unestablished in attribution. Four versions were found. (1) Brohier, the standard authority on Ceylon's canals, attributes the first cut to the Portuguese in 1505-1656 and says its purpose was to divert river floodwater away from the paddy, not to drain the marsh; on his account it was that cut which unintentionally opened a passage for sea water. (2) Several secondary and travel sources attribute the first canal network to Veera Parakramabahu VIII of Kotte (1477-1496), cut to move areca nut, cloves, cardamom, pepper and cinnamon, and say the resulting salt intrusion destroyed the paddy. (3) The account most often encountered says the Dutch attempted paddy here between 1658 and 1795 and were defeated by the tides, as Sinhalese kings had been before them — this version does not claim the Dutch cut caused the salinity. (4) The English Wikipedia article attaches the counter-productive effect to the British canal of 1802-04, which was built to drain salt water and which it says 'created the opposite effect, as the coastal tides brought increasing salinity not only from Negombo Lagoon but also the Kelani Ganga'. The brief's own framing — a Dutch-period drainage attempt that failed and let salt water in — is therefore the weakest of the four attributions. The film should say that a cut was made to improve this ground and let the sea into it, name the colonial power only where the source it is following names one, and not assign the blame.

Who conceived the British canal. Wikipedia names George Atkinson, Colonial Surveyor General, as its author, with Gavin Hamilton supporting; Brohier-based accounts and most others have Hamilton himself supervising or conceiving it. Wikipedia also prints Hamilton's dates as '(1494-1803)', which is plainly corrupt, and gives no birth year that can be relied on.

The nickname. 'Moda Ela' (fool's canal) and 'Hamilton's Folly' are asserted on many travel pages, blogs and aggregators in near-identical wording, and appear in none of the Brohier-based accounts nor in the 2023 Sunday Observer feature on the canal. Treat as reported usage, not as established.

Lengths and counts. The British canal is given as 14.5 km, but the wider system it joined is given as 172 km, as about 193 km plus 24 km across the Puttalam lagoon, and as 'more than 125 kilometres'. The expressway is 25.8 km in most sources and 'approximately 24.6 km' in the supervising consultant's own project note; its culverts are given as 88 and as 102; its construction start is given as October 2009 and as 18 August 2009. Wikipedia's marsh article reports '209 distinct species of fauna ... as well as another 102 species of birds', which double-counts the birds: in the IUCN survey the 102 birds are inside the 209.

The age of the marsh. 'About 5000 years BC' in the IUCN paper, following CEA/Euroconsult 1994; 'about 7,000 years ago' in the Wikipedia article. These are compatible but not identical claims and the second is looser.

Ramsar status. The marsh is not among Sri Lanka's six Ramsar sites, and the 2021 gazette spoke of a step towards declaring one; nonetheless several sources describe it as a Ramsar wetland and at least one explicitly denies it. Unsettled in the public record and not to be asserted either way.

How much of the crossing is actually on legs. The elevated structures that can be named are the 480 m viaduct at Hunupitiya and the 800 m viaduct at Katunayake, plus 42 bridges 'built mostly over the marshes'; a major part of the route is embankment founded on treated peat rather than deck on piers. Whether a boat can pass beneath a pier line inside the marsh proper, as against at a river or lagoon crossing, is unverified and is a recce question.

The current legal position. What became of the 7 October 2021 gazette after the review committee, whether the sanctuary boundaries were ever demarcated, the status of the LNG power project land and of the company's private claims inside the wetland were not established beyond 2021-2022 reporting. Anything stated on screen about the present-day dispute must be re-checked at the time of filming.

what_to_film: A long slow move at boat height inside a reed channel, held far past comfort, with no horizon and nothing above head height, so the viewer loses orientation before the film says a word about it.
The climb out of that channel in one unbroken move, from no-orientation to the whole maze, which is the film's hinge.
The maze from directly overhead in first light, wide enough that it has no centre and no edge.
The old canal from above, running straight across the frame and ignoring every bend in the peat on either side of it.
The two canal lines together if they can be framed: the British cut of 1802-04 nearer the sea and the older line east of it, two answers two centuries apart running side by side.

The expressway from two positions: the deck at traffic speed, and the underside from a boat passing between the piers at one of the water crossings. Establish on the recce where a pier line is actually reachable by boat, because much of the crossing is embankment on treated peat rather than deck on legs.
The stretch where the expressway runs along the line of the old canal, which is the newest answer laid on top of the oldest.
One high wide frame carrying all three routes at once with a working boat somewhere in it. Everything else is built around getting this.
A channel grown shut and a channel newly open, filmed the same morning, as the plain evidence that the routes genuinely differ by season.
Ordinary work on the water in flat daylight: traps lifted, a channel poled, two boats passing and one crew calling across to another. Brush piles, cast nets and drift nets are the recorded gear here.
The dry-season interface if the timing allows: the marsh-lagoon transition where salt comes back up the canals when the freshwater flow drops. Nothing dramatic to see, which is the point.
Dusk: black marsh, silver canal, the expressway lamps coming on in a line above it, birds going down into the reeds.
suggested_location.access: By road from the airport highway or the coast road, then by small boat. There is a visitor centre with boat access at the southern end, run in connection with the sanctuary, and working boats go in from the fishing settlements along the lagoon; the film needs the second rather than the first, which means arranging with people who are going out anyway. The northern 1,777 ha is a declared sanctuary under the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance (Gazette 947/13, July 1996) administered by the Department of Wildlife Conservation, so filming and any aerial work will need wildlife-authority permission; an additional complication is that the sanctuary's physical boundaries were never marked on the ground, which was still the subject of a Court of Appeal direction to the Surveyor General as of 2021, so where the protected area begins may not be answerable locally. Parts of the southern marsh are also an Environmental Protection Area under the Central Environmental Authority. Drone flight near an expressway and inside the approach corridor of an international airport is a separate and probably harder permission.
suggested_location.best_time: The first hour after sunrise for mist on the channels, and the last hour before dark for the canal and the expressway lights. A falling tide opens the most channel. The two monsoon shoulders give the sharpest contrast between one month's routes and the next; annual rainfall here is 2,000-2,500 mm, and the low-rain months are when salt water pushes furthest back up the canals into the marsh, which is the film's oldest story still happening.

suggested_location.research_note: Rebuilt on sourced material 2026-09-25. The load-bearing figures now come from two IUCN publications rather than from tour operators: Bambaradeniya et al., 'An Assessment of the Status of Biodiversity in the Muthurajawela Wetland Sanctuary' (IUCN Sri Lanka Occasional Paper 3, 2002), for the marsh's extent, hydrology, species counts, water quality and threats; and Emerton and Kekulandala, 'Assessment of the Economic Value of Muthurajawela Wetland' (IUCN 2003), for the population, the fishery, the soil's present unfitness for cultivation, the master plan zoning and the valuation. The earlier figure of 'about 6,000 hectares' was loose and has been replaced: the marsh is 3,068 ha and the 6,232 ha figure belongs to the marsh and lagoon together. The canal history is from the Brohier-based account on AmazingLanka (citing Links Between Sri Lanka and the Netherlands 1978, Ancient Irrigation Works in Ceylon 1980 and Discovering Ceylon 1982) checked against the English Wikipedia article, which is the source of Gavin Hamilton's career, his death in February 1803 and the £19,675; the two disagree on who conceived the canal and on which colonial power's cut admitted the sea, and both disagreements are recorded rather than resolved. Three things the earlier note asserted have been corrected. First, the canal through the marsh is not simply 'cut by the British on an older Dutch line': the British cut a second, parallel canal nearer the sea, and the older line still exists separately. Second, the expressway does not cross the marsh entirely on piers. A major part of its 25.8 km is embankment on peat treated by pre-loading, prefabricated vertical drains, sand compaction piles and stone columns; the named elevated structures are a 480 m viaduct at Hunupitiya and an 800 m viaduct at Katunayake, with 42 bridges mostly over marsh. The film's picture of a road on legs over the whole marsh is an overstatement of the record and the recce must establish where a pier line is genuinely reachable by boat. Third, the name's meaning is unsettled and the popular glosses are unsourced. Everything about access remains desk research: no boat, family, wildlife-authority permission, aviation clearance or sanctuary boundary has been verified, and the sanctuary's boundaries were still undemarcated in the most recent reporting found. The coordinates are an approximate point inside the marsh, not a surveyed position. Images: all six files were confirmed to exist through the Commons query API before their URLs were written. Commons holds almost nothing shot inside the marsh itself — two files, one of them a small photograph of a monitor lizard which was left out — so the canal and expressway pictures are of those structures elsewhere along their length and each caption says so.

unknowns: No boat, family or access has been found or approached. Everything here is a research direction.
Whether the maze, the canal and the elevated road can actually be held in one frame, at a legal and safe altitude, is unverified and decides whether the film has its central image.

Where along the expressway a pier line stands in water reachable by a small boat, as against a bank on treated ground. The two viaducts that can be named are at the southern and northern ends, not in the middle of the marsh.
Whether the two canal lines, the British cut of 1802-04 and the older line east of it, are both still open water where the film would work, and whether they can be framed together.
Whether the channels genuinely change enough between seasons to show a route closed and a route opened is desk inference and needs checking with people who work the water.
Drone permission over a declared wetland sanctuary, near an expressway and inside an airport approach corridor is unverified and may be refused on any one of the three grounds.

Where the sanctuary boundary actually runs. It was gazetted in 1996 and had still not been marked on the ground in the most recent reporting found, which makes the permission question harder to answer locally, not easier.

The current state of the disputes: what became of the 2021 gazette after the review committee, whether demarcation happened, and the status of the power-project land and of private claims inside the wetland. Nothing was established past 2021-2022 reporting and it must be re-checked before filming.
How much of the marsh has been filled or encroached since the sanctuary was declared, and whether that changes what the film would honestly be showing.
